title: Ibn Kathir
hookLine: a commentary explaining the Qur'an by the Qur'an and hadith
tomorrow: a verse about washing your hands. where's the law in it?

lines: SCROLL UP: SHE ALREADY SAID IT.
cards: A friend drops a word in the group chat you don't understand. Before you ask, you scroll up, and there it is: she explained it a few messages back.
Ibn Kathir, a scholar of Damascus, opens his commentary with that same rule. The best way to explain the Qur'an is by the Qur'an: what one place says briefly, another spells out.
If that isn't enough, go to the Sunna, the Prophet's own teaching. Then to his companions, then to their students. The book explains itself, first.

teach.h: THE SAME WORDS OPEN AL IMRAN.
teach.b: Watch him do it with the verse of the Throne, Ayat al-Kursi. It opens: "Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal."
Ibn Kathir notes those same words open another surah, Al Imran, so one passage lights the other.
Then a hadith: the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, asked his companion Ubayy ibn Ka'b which verse of the book is greatest.
Ubayy said this one, and the Prophet struck him on the chest and said, may knowledge delight you. Now the debate inside the tradition.
One side, Ibn Kathir's: start with the Qur'an and the reports, because reasoning alone can read yourself into the text. He cites a hadith warning against speaking about the Qur'an by mere opinion.
The other side, commentators who give reason a bigger room: the Qur'an itself asks people to ponder it, and reports don't answer every question a new age asks.
Reason, carefully used, is part of obeying the book. Notice how much they share.
Both begin with the Qur'an. Both use reports and reasoning. They differ on which leads, and how far reasoning may go.

how: Ibn Kathir's tafsir is read in mosques, study circles and homes, in Arabic and in translation; hadith encourage reciting Ayat al-Kursi after the daily prayers and before sleep.

o: a scholar who explains the Qur'an by the Qur'an first
a caliph of Damascus who built a great mosque
a poet who wrote verses in praise of the Throne

games.q: Ibn Kathir's order — tap the pairs.

s: Ibn Kathir says the best way to explain the Qur'an is by the Qur'an
what one place says briefly, another spells out.
commentators who give reason a bigger role ignore the hadith
both sides use reports and reasoning; they differ on which leads.
Ayat al-Kursi's opening words appear in another surah too
Al Imran opens the same way, and Ibn Kathir points it out.

games.q: your study circle splits: one friend says stick to the transmitted reports; another says reason has a big role. you're asked to give the reports side's best case. what is it?
o: reasoning is forbidden in Islam, so thinking about verses is wrong.
old reports are simpler, so they're easier for everyone to follow.
reason alone can read you into the text; reports keep you close to it.
games.why: that's Ibn Kathir's worry, and the other side's best case is just as real: the Qur'an asks people to ponder it, and new questions need careful reason.

practice: If you know Ayat al-Kursi in Arabic, say it softly, once, slowly. If not, say its opening in English, one phrase per breath: Allah, there is no God save him, the Alive, the Eternal. Let each phrase finish before the next begins.
